claim: CTCF was originally identified as a candidate transcription regulator of c-myc.
source: Originally identified as a candidate transcription regulator of c-myc, this multi zinc finger protein is highly conserved amongst Nephrozoa (Heger et al., 2012; Lobanenkov et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Heger et al., 2012 and Lobanenkov et al., 1990.

claim: CTCF is a multi zinc finger protein highly conserved amongst Nephrozoa.
source: Originally identified as a candidate transcription regulator of c-myc, this multi zinc finger protein is highly conserved amongst Nephrozoa (Heger et al., 2012; Lobanenkov et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Heger et al., 2012 and Lobanenkov et al., 1990.

claim: CTCF has insulatory activity, specifically in blocking enhancer-promoter interactions.
source: Subsequent studies further revealed that CTCF has insulatory activity, specifically in blocking enhancer-promoter interactions, and in separating transcriptionally active genomic regions from heterochromatic domains (Merkenschlager and Odom, 2013; Ong and Corces, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Merkenschlager and Odom, 2013 and Ong and Corces, 2014.

claim: CTCF separates transcriptionally active genomic regions from heterochromatic domains.
source: Subsequent studies further revealed that CTCF has insulatory activity, specifically in blocking enhancer-promoter interactions, and in separating transcriptionally active genomic regions from heterochromatic domains (Merkenschlager and Odom, 2013; Ong and Corces, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Merkenschlager and Odom, 2013 and Ong and Corces, 2014.

claim: Mammalian genomes contain tens of thousands of CTCF binding sites.
source: Later genomic studies revealed tens of thousands of CTCF binding sites in mammalian genomes (Kim et al., 2007; Rhee and Pugh, 2011; Nakahashi et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2007), with >5000 of these being conserved (Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies: Kim et al., 2007; Rhee and Pugh, 2011; Nakahashi et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2007.

claim: More than 5000 CTCF binding sites are conserved in mammalian genomes.
source: Later genomic studies revealed tens of thousands of CTCF binding sites in mammalian genomes (Kim et al., 2007; Rhee and Pugh, 2011; Nakahashi et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2007), with >5000 of these being conserved (Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2012.

claim: CTCF plays an architectural role in shaping the genome by helping to mediate three-dimensional chromatin loops.
source: In addition to CTCF's role in blocking enhancer-promoter loops, recent chromatin conformation capture (3C) based assays revealed that CTCF paradoxically also plays an architectural role in shaping the genome as well, helping to mediate three-dimensional chromatin loops in some cases.
evidence: The claim is based on chromatin conformation capture (3C) based assays mentioned in the text.

claim: CTCF binds to the borders of many Topologically Associating Domains (TADs).
source: In addition, 3C-based assays also revealed that CTCF binds to the borders of many Topologically Associating Domains (TADs), megabase-sized regions which function to insulate chromatin interactions such as promoter-enhancer loops (Ong and Corces, 2014; Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ong and Corces, 2014; Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012.

claim: TADs are megabase-sized regions which function to insulate chromatin interactions such as promoter-enhancer loops.
source: In addition, 3C-based assays also revealed that CTCF binds to the borders of many Topologically Associating Domains (TADs), megabase-sized regions which function to insulate chromatin interactions such as promoter-enhancer loops (Ong and Corces, 2014; Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ong and Corces, 2014; Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012.

claim: Disruption of TADs through deletion of CTCF sites can lead to genetic disease through ectopic enhancer-mediated upregulation of genes.
source: Disruption of TADs, for example through deletion of CTCF sites, can lead to genetic disease through ectopic enhancer-mediated upregulation of genes (Lupiáñez et al., 2015; Rao et al., 2014; Sanborn et al., 2015; Nora et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lupiáñez et al., 2015; Rao et al., 2014; Sanborn et al., 2015; Nora et al., 2017.

claim: Poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation of CTCF plays roles in imprinting and nucleolar transcription.
source: Poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation of CTCF has been found to play roles in imprinting and nucleolar transcription (Torrano et al., 2006; Yu et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Torrano et al., 2006 and Yu et al., 2004.

claim: SUMOylation of CTCF appears to enhance its repressive function.
source: while SUMOylation of CTCF appears to enhance its repressive function (MacPherson et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to MacPherson et al., 2009.

claim: Phosphorylation of CTCF has been proposed to turn CTCF into a transcription activator.
source: Finally, phosphorylation of CTCF has been proposed to turn CTCF into a transcription activator (El-Kady and Klenova, 2005) or reduce its DNA-binding activity (Sekiya et al., 2017), depending on site.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to El-Kady and Klenova, 2005.

claim: Phosphorylation of CTCF has been proposed to reduce its DNA-binding activity, depending on site.
source: Finally, phosphorylation of CTCF has been proposed to turn CTCF into a transcription activator (El-Kady and Klenova, 2005) or reduce its DNA-binding activity (Sekiya et al., 2017), depending on site.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sekiya et al., 2017.

claim: Several proteomic screens have identified CTCF phosphorylation sites using mass spectrometry.
source: Several proteomic screens have been carried out using mass spectrometry (Rigbolt et al., 2011; Olsen et al., 2010; Kettenbach et al., 2011; Dephoure et al., 2008), though phosphorylation sites were called by confidence scores made by probabilistic scoring algorithms without further validation or characterization.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rigbolt et al., 2011; Olsen et al., 2010; Kettenbach et al., 2011; Dephoure et al., 2008.

claim: Murine CTCF is phosphorylated at Serine 224.
source: A unique murine site of serine phosphorylation was identified at Ser224, which is ~50 aa N-terminal of the CTCF zinc finger domain (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: CTCF Ser224 is approximately 50 amino acids N-terminal of the CTCF zinc finger domain.
source: A unique murine site of serine phosphorylation was identified at Ser224, which is ~50 aa N-terminal of the CTCF zinc finger domain (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is based on the location of Ser224 relative to the zinc finger domain as stated in the text.

claim: A single peptide containing human CTCF Ser224-P was identified in a phosphoproteome screen of HeLa cells.
source: Notably, in a phosphoproteome screen of HeLa cells, a single peptide containing human CTCF Ser224-P was identified (Kettenbach et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kettenbach et al., 2011.

claim: CTCF orthologs have only been found in Nephrozoa.
source: Interestingly, CTCF orthologs have only been found in Nephrozoa (Heger et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Heger et al., 2012.

claim: The CTCF amino acid sequence surrounding Ser224 shows striking conservation amongst vertebrata.
source: A 25 amino acid window centered on mouse Ser224 remarkably revealed striking conservation proximal to this position amongst vertebrata, but not echinodermata or arthropoda (arrow, Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The CTCF amino acid sequence surrounding Ser224 does not show conservation in echinodermata or arthropoda.
source: A 25 amino acid window centered on mouse Ser224 remarkably revealed striking conservation proximal to this position amongst vertebrata, but not echinodermata or arthropoda (arrow, Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The conservation of CTCF Ser224 suggests that phosphorylation is potentially catalyzed by a conserved vertebrate kinase.
source: This conservation suggests that Ser224 phosphorylation is potentially catalyzed by a conserved vertebrate kinase.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the conservation pattern observed in the sequence alignment.

claim: Casein kinase 2 (CK2) can phosphorylate CTCF in vitro at Ser604, Ser609, Ser610 and Ser612.
source: It was previously reported that casein kinase 2 (CK2) could phosphorylate CTCF in vitro at Ser604, Ser609, Ser610 and Ser612 (Klenova et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Klenova et al., 2001.

claim: The amino acid sequence surrounding CTCF Ser224 fits the known CK2 recognition site (S-x-x-D/E).
source: Interestingly, the highly conserved amino acid sequence surrounding Ser224 fits the known CK2 recognition site (S-x-x-D/E) (Figure 1F) (Meggio and Pinna, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Meggio and Pinna, 2003 and the sequence shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Recombinant CTCF can be phosphorylated by CK2.
source: Following SDS-PAGE, autoradiography revealed that recombinant CTCF can be phosphorylated by CK2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the autoradiography data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CK2 phosphorylates CTCF at Ser224.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis of the band, revealed that CKII phosphorylated CTCF Ser224 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The CTCF Ser224-P antibody has reduced affinity for phosphatase treated samples.
source: western blot revealed that the CTCF Ser224-P antibody had reduced affinity for the phosphatase treated samples (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The CTCF Ser224-P antibody recognizes a smaller (~125 kDa) band that is not detected by a CTCF monoclonal antibody.
source: The CTCF Ser224-P antibody also recognizes a smaller (~125 kDa) band that is not detected by a CTCF monoclonal antibody (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CTCF migrates at a higher molecular weight (150 kDa) than predicted (84 kDa) in SDS-PAGE gels.
source: Notably CTCF migrates at a higher molecular weight (150 kDa) than predicted (84 kDa) in SDS-PAGE gels.
evidence: The claim is based on observed migration patterns in SDS-PAGE gels.

claim: The CTCF Ser224-P antibody prefers CK2 phosphorylated CTCF over unphosphorylated CTCF.
source: While the western blot revealed some affinity of the CTCF Ser224-P antibody for unphosphorylated CTCF; the antibody preferred the CK2 phosphorylated protein (2nd column, Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The CTCF Ser224-P antibody is likely reactive to Ser224-P rather than other potential CK2 phosphorylation sites.
source: Moreover, the antibody is likely reactive to Ser224-P rather than other potential CK2 phosphorylation sites as there appeared to be no bias to CK2 phosphorylated S224A or S224E (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CTCF Ser224-P localizes in a pattern reminiscent of total CTCF in the nucleus.
source: Using immortalized tetraploid female MEFs, we found that the CTCF Ser224-P antibody labeled a nuclear antigen in a pattern reminiscent of CTCF (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CTCF is visually excluded during interphase from nucleoli and constitutive heterochromatic regions.
source: Furthermore, CTCF was visually excluded during interphase from nucleoli and constitutive heterochromatic regions (Burke et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Burke et al., 2005.

claim: CTCF Ser224-P is not enriched on the inactive X chromosome.
source: CTCF Ser224-P was not enriched on the Xi, and we found no evident visual distinction between CTCF Ser224-P and total CTCF nuclear distribution regardless of co-staining nucleoli and heterochromatin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: At a cytological level, CTCF Ser224-P appears to distribute similarly as total CTCF in the nucleus.
source: Thus, at a cytological level, CTCF Ser224-P appears to distribute similarly as total CTCF in the nucleus.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on immunofluorescence observations.

claim: CTCF Ser224-P labeling is not homogeneous in an asynchronous population of MEFs.
source: However, a remarkable observation from our immunofluorescence assays was that CTCF Ser224-P labeling was not homogeneous in an asynchronous population of MEFs.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence observations.

claim: Some nuclei are more intensely labeled by the CTCF Ser224-P antibody whereas nuclei stained with total CTCF antibody are uniformly labeled.
source: Some of the nuclei were more intensely labeled by the CTCF Ser224-P antibody whereas nuclei stained with total CTCF antibody were uniformly labeled (arrows, Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A subset of asynchronous HEK293 cells is intensely labeled by the CTCF Ser224-P antibody.
source: As predicted, CTCF Ser224-P labeling of asynchronous HEK293 revealed that a subset of cells was intensely labeled by the antibody (arrows, Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 23.4% of asynchronous MEFs are CTCF Ser224-P positive.
source: While a total CTCF antibody labeled 100% of the cells (n = 104), again only a fraction of the cells (23.4%, n = 248) were CTCF Ser224-P positive (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 94.8% of CTCF Ser224-P positive cells are co-labeled with H3S10ph antibody.
source: Comparing this fraction to the cell cycle markers revealed that a striking majority (94.8%) of the CTCF Ser224-P positive cells were co-labeled with H3S10ph antibody (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CTCF Ser224-P labeling is most prominent in cells in both early G2 and late G2/prophase.
source: The CTCF Ser224-P labeling was most prominent in cells in both early G2 and late G2/prophase, as evidenced from the H3S10ph staining pattern (white arrows, early G2; yellow arrows, late G2/prophase. Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Phosphorylation of CTCF Ser224 likely initiates at the end of S phase and peaks at G2/M.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that phosphorylation of CTCF Ser224 likely initiates at the end of S phase and peaks at G2/M.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on immunofluorescence data showing co-staining with cell cycle markers.

claim: RO-3306 treatment results in an accumulation of CTCF Ser224-P positive cells blocked at G2/M.
source: RO-3306 treatment resulted in an accumulation of CTCF Ser224-P positive cells blocked at G2/M as evident from the concomitant increase in H3S10ph co-staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: PLK1 is a regulator of the G2/M transition and phosphorylates mitosis-associated substrates.
source: PLK1 is a regulator of the G2/M transition and phosphorylates mitosis-associated substrates (Barr et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Barr et al., 2004.

claim: PLK1 expression increases from S phase and peaks during G2.
source: Importantly, PLK1 expression increases from S phase and peaks during G2 (Golsteyn et al., 1994; Lake and Jelinek, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Golsteyn et al., 1994 and Lake and Jelinek, 1993.

claim: CTCF Ser224 is a potential target of PLK1 based on the consensus PLK1 substrate site.
source: Comparing the consensus PLK1 substrate site to the amino acid sequence flanking CTCF Ser224 revealed that Ser224 is a potential target of PLK1 (Figure 3A) (Nakajima et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to the consensus PLK1 substrate site shown in Figure 3A and citation to Nakajima et al., 2003.

claim: PLK1 conservation mirrors that of its potential CTCF Ser224 substrate, where the kinase is most conserved amongst vertebrates.
source: We found that PLK1 conservation mirrors that of its potential CTCF Ser224 substrate, where the kinase is most conserved amongst vertebrates (Figures 1F and 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the conservation analysis shown in Figures 1F and 3B.

claim: Treatment with 100 nM BI 6727 reduces the percentage of CTCF Ser224-P positive cells from 30.8% to 18.3%.
source: While 30.8% (n = 214) of untreated cells were CTCF Ser224-P positive, only 18.3% (n = 175) were positive following treatment with 100 nM BI 6727 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Treatment with 1000 nM BI 6727 completely ablates CTCF Ser224-P phosphorylation.
source: Supporting this, 1000 nM BI 6727 completely ablated CTCF Ser224-P phosphorylation (n = 101) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Total CTCF expression is not affected by 12 hr treatment with BI 6726 at either 100 nM or 1000 nM concentration.
source: Total CTCF expression was not affected by 12 hr treatment with BI 6726 at either concentration (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PLK1 directly phosphorylates CTCF in vitro.
source: In support of our hypothesis, we found that PLK1 directly phosphorylated CTCF (*, Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PLK1 phosphorylates CTCF at Ser224 in vitro.
source: Analysis by mass spectrometry revealed phosphorylation at Ser224, arguing that indeed PLK1 is the kinase for CTCF Ser224 (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CTCF remains bound to mitotic chromosomes – both along the dyad arms and at centromeres.
source: It was previously reported that CTCF remains bound to mitotic chromosomes – both along the dyad arms and at centromeres (Burke et al., 2005; Rubio et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burke et al., 2005 and Rubio et al., 2008.

claim: CTCF is phosphorylated in its zinc finger domain during mitosis which results in its dissociation from chromatids.
source: However it was also reported that CTCF is phosphorylated in its zinc finger domain during mitosis which results in its dissociation from chromatids (Sekiya et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sekiya et al., 2017.

claim: CTCF Ser224-P can be observed on chromatid arms during metaphase.
source: Much like CTCF, CTCF Ser224-P could be observed on chromatid arms, albeit not uniformly like CTCF (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: CTCF Ser224-P is enriched in pericentric regions between the centromeres and the H3K27me3 positive dyad arms during metaphase.
source: Remarkably, CTCF Ser224-P appeared distinctly enriched in between the centromeres of the murine acrocentric chromosomes and the H3K27me3 positive dyad arms.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence observations comparing CTCF Ser224-P and H3K27me3 staining.

claim: The metaphase localization of CTCF Ser224-P is pericentric.
source: We therefore concluded that the metaphase localization of CTCF Ser224-P is pericentric (Figure 3G–H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3G–H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Approximately 50,000 CTCF peaks were detected genome-wide in TST-1 mESCs.
source: From our CTCF ChIP-seq, we detected ~50,000 CTCF peaks genome-wide (z = 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: 54% of CTCF ChIP-seq peaks show significant enrichment of CTCF motifs centered in the peaks.
source: MEME-ChIP analysis tellingly revealed significant enrichment of CTCF motifs (JASPAR MA0139.1) centered in these peaks (54% of peaks, p=3.0e-10948) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) (Bailey et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by MEME-ChIP analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and citation to Bailey et al., 2009.

claim: Approximately 900 CTCF Ser224-P peaks were detected in CTCF Ser224-P ChIP-seq.
source: In contrast, only ~900 CTCF Ser224-P peaks were detected in our CTCF Ser224-P ChIP-seq (z = 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: 48% of CTCF Ser224-P peaks contain a significantly enriched motif that closely matches the CTCF motif.
source: Using MEME-ChIP, we de novo identified a significantly enriched motif in the CTCF Ser224-P peaks (48% of peaks, p=2.7e-88) that closely matched the CTCF motif (p=1.8e-86) and was likewise centered in the peaks (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by MEME-ChIP analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The genomic feature distribution of CTCF Ser224-P peaks is broadly similar to that of CTCF peaks.
source: Further CEAS analysis of the CTCF Ser224-P peaks revealed a genomic feature distribution that was also broadly similar to that of CTCF peaks (Figure 4B) (Shin et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by CEAS analysis shown in Figure 4B and citation to Shin et al., 2009.

claim: 95.9% of CTCF Ser224-P peaks intersect with CTCF peaks.
source: Notably, the vast majority (95.9%) of the CTCF Ser224-P peaks intersected with our CTCF peaks (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq peak intersection analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CTCF Ser224-P peaks are proximal to both transcribed and non-transcribed regions.
source: And comparison to mESC RNA-seq data (GSM723776) revealed that CTCF Ser224-P peaks were also proximal to both transcribed and non-transcribed regions (Figure 4C) (Shen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C and citation to Shen et al., 2012.

claim: The linear relationship between CTCF Ser224-P and CTCF binding signal explains about half of all CTCF Ser224-P binding.
source: While there was a detectable linear relationship between CTCF Ser224-P and CTCF binding signal, this was only sufficient to explain about half of all CTCF Ser224-P binding (R2, fraction of variation in CTCF Ser224-P binding explained by CTCF binding, for all peaks = 0.48, R2 for shared peaks = 0.54).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: At least a subset of CTCF Ser224-P ChIP-seq peaks likely represent real binding sites outside of pericentric regions.
source: Therefore, at least a subset of CTCF Ser224-P ChIP-seq peaks likely represented real binding sites outside of pericentric regions.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the correlation analysis showing that antibody cross-reactivity cannot fully explain all CTCF Ser224-P binding.

claim: Shared CTCF and CTCF Ser224-P ChIP peaks have significantly more CTCF binding signal than CTCF peaks in general.
source: Shared CTCF and CTCF Ser224-P ChIP peaks (representing 95.9% of all CTCF Ser224-P peaks) had significantly more CTCF binding signal than CTCF peaks in general (Figure 4E, p<2.2e-16, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CTCF Ser224-P ChIP peaks tend to contain more motifs than CTCF ChIP peaks.
source: While CTCF motifs found in CTCF Ser224-P peaks did not tend to be more conserved than motifs found in CTCF ChIP peaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, p=0.1623, Wilcoxon rank sum test), CTCFSer224-P ChIP peaks did tend to contain more motifs than CTCF ChIP peaks (Figure 4F, p<2.2e-16, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: CTCF Ser224-P ChIP peaks tend to be found at higher affinity sites with greater numbers of CTCF binding sites than CTCF ChIP peaks in general.
source: In other words, CTCFSer224-P ChIP peaks tend to be found at higher affinity sites with greater numbers of CTCF binding sites than CTCF ChIP peaks in general.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that CTCF Ser224-P peaks have more CTCF binding signal and more motifs.

claim: 51.6% of CTCF Ser224-P ChIP peaks overlap with SMC1 peaks.
source: While 22.8% and 33.3% of our CTCF ChIP-seq peaks overlapped with SMC1 and SMC3 peaks, respectively, 51.6% and 85.1% of our CTCFSer224-P ChIP peaks overlapped with SMC1 and SMC3 peaks, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to previously published cohesin ChIP-seq data.

claim: 85.1% of CTCF Ser224-P ChIP peaks overlap with SMC3 peaks.
source: While 22.8% and 33.3% of our CTCF ChIP-seq peaks overlapped with SMC1 and SMC3 peaks, respectively, 51.6% and 85.1% of our CTCFSer224-P ChIP peaks overlapped with SMC1 and SMC3 peaks, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to previously published cohesin ChIP-seq data.

claim: CTCF Ser224-P ChIP tends to co-bind more frequently with cohesin.
source: This suggests that CTCFSer224-P ChIP tends to co-bind more frequently with cohesin as well.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the higher overlap of CTCF Ser224-P peaks with cohesin peaks.

claim: Overexpression of S224E but not wild type or S224A affects growth of mESCs.
source: Ectopic expression of S224E but not wild type or S224A affected growth of mESCs (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony growth data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: mESC colonies overexpressing S224E for 6 days have significantly smaller diameters than uninduced cells.
source: Namely, mESC colonies overexpressing S224E for 6 days had significantly smaller diameters than uninduced cells, while overexpressing wild type or S224A did not result in significantly smaller colonies (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony diameter quantification shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression levels of FLAG-tagged CTCF, S224A, and S224E are comparable in all clones.
source: Expression levels of the induced FLAG-tagged proteins were comparable in all clones by western blot (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CTCF Ser224 mutations (S224A and S224E) do not affect nuclear localization of CTCF.
source: Regardless of either amino acid substitution at Ser224, nuclear localization of CTCF was not affected. (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Both S224A and S224E mutants bind to a known CTCF motif and not to a mutated motif.
source: As expected, regardless of amino acid polarity or charge, both mutants bound the known CTCF motif and not the mutated motif (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Overexpression of S224A or S224E does not lead to defects in cell cycle progression.
source: We generated DNA content profiles of mESCs with inducible wild-type CTCF, S224A, or S224E transgenes after six days of doxycycline induction and did not observe any blockages in the cell cycle (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle profile data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type or mutant CTCF does not lead to significantly higher numbers of polyploid spreads.
source: However, we did not find significantly higher numbers of polyploid spreads in mESCs overexpressing wild-type or mutant CTCF versus uninduced mESCs (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by karyotyping data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: Many CTCF Ser224-P ChIP-seq peaks overlap CTCF peaks at the borders of Topologically Associating Domains (TADs).
source: We first noted that many of our CTCF Ser224-P ChIP-seq peaks detected in interphase overlapped CTCF peaks at the borders of Topologically Associating Domains (TADs) (Figure 8A), megabase-scale organizational structures on chromosomes within which genetic elements show high frequency of interaction (Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 8A and citations to Dixon et al., 2012 and Nora et al., 2012.

claim: The Mecp2 TAD score is similar with or without overexpression of wild type CTCF, S224A and S224E.
source: The Mecp2 TAD score was similar with or without overexpression of wild type CTCF, S224A and S224E.
evidence: The claim is supported by TAD score analysis of Hi-C2 data.

claim: Overexpression of CTCF, including CTCF S224E, does not detectably impact three-dimensional chromatin structure.
source: Thus, overexpression of CTCF, including CTCF S224E, does not detectably impact three-dimensional chromatin structure (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C2 and TAD score analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: 375 genes are differentially expressed when CTCF S224E is induced in mESCs.
source: We found 375 genes that were DE between two replicates (adjusted p-value<0.01), with 118 (31%) being upregulated and 257 (69%) being downregulated upon overexpression of CTCF S224E (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 8C (note: the text refers to Figure 8C but likely means Figure 8D based on the MA plot description).

claim: 118 genes are upregulated upon overexpression of CTCF S224E.
source: We found 375 genes that were DE between two replicates (adjusted p-value<0.01), with 118 (31%) being upregulated and 257 (69%) being downregulated upon overexpression of CTCF S224E (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 257 genes are downregulated upon overexpression of CTCF S224E.
source: We found 375 genes that were DE between two replicates (adjusted p-value<0.01), with 118 (31%) being upregulated and 257 (69%) being downregulated upon overexpression of CTCF S224E (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: CTCF is not a differentially expressed gene upon overexpression of CTCF S224E.
source: Surprisingly, CTCF was not a DE gene.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 12–16% of RNA-seq reads overlapping CTCF codon 224 have the glutamate codon at position 224.
source: To confirm that CTCF S224E was expressed, we examined RNA-seq reads overlapping CTCF codon 224 and found that 12–16% of reads had the glutamate codon at position 224 (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq read analysis shown in Figure 8D (note: the text refers to Figure 8D but likely means Figure 8E based on the description).

claim: CTCF binding is enriched along both downregulated and upregulated differentially expressed genes.
source: On average, CTCF binding was enriched along both downregulated and upregulated DE genes, albeit at different locations.
evidence: The claim is supported by metagene coverage analysis of ChIP-seq data over DE genes.

claim: Downregulated genes are more enriched in CTCF binding upstream of the transcription start site.
source: In particular, downregulated genes were more enriched in CTCF binding upstream of the transcription start site, while upregulated genes were more enriched in CTCF binding along the gene body.

source: Among upregulated genes, the only significantly overrepresented PANTHER pathway was the p53 pathway (FDR = 0.0495), most notably including Trp53 (upregulated 1.3-fold, adjusted p-value<0.00075) and Cdkn1a (upregulated 1.3-fold, adjusted p-value<0.00043), genes which were also bound by CTCF and CTCF Ser224-P (Figure 8F).
evidence: The claim is supported by PANTHER overrepresentation analysis and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8F (note: the text refers to Figure 8F but likely means Figure 8G based on the description).

claim: Modest CTCF S224E overexpression could lead to the slight activation of p53 signaling.

claim: The serine 224 of CTCF plays a critical role in regulating gene expression.
source: We conclude that the serine 224 of CTCF plays a critical role in regulating gene expression and suggest that the effect on the p53 signaling pathway may partly explain the growth phenotype in mESCs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed gene expression changes upon S224E overexpression.

claim: The effect of CTCF S224E on the p53 signaling pathway may partly explain the growth phenotype in mESCs.
source: We conclude that the serine 224 of CTCF plays a critical role in regulating gene expression and suggest that the effect on the p53 signaling pathway may partly explain the growth phenotype in mESCs.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the observed upregulation of p53 pathway genes and the growth phenotype.

claim: CTCF is differentially regulated during the cell cycle, with CTCF Ser224-P being enriched at G2/M.
source: Here we discovered and confirmed a CTCF PTM conserved among vertebrates. We observe for the first time that CTCF is differentially regulated during the cell cycle, with CTCF Ser224-P being enriched at G2/M and specifically on pericentric regions during metaphase.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing CTCF Ser224-P enrichment in G2/M cells.

claim: CTCF Ser224-P is specifically enriched on pericentric regions during metaphase.
source: Here we discovered and confirmed a CTCF PTM conserved among vertebrates. We observe for the first time that CTCF is differentially regulated during the cell cycle, with CTCF Ser224-P being enriched at G2/M and specifically on pericentric regions during metaphase.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data on metaphase chromosomes.

claim: CTCF Ser224 phosphorylation is regulated by the kinase PLK1.
source: Notably, CTCF Ser224 phosphorylation is regulated by the kinase PLK1 whose expression profile also peaks in G2/M.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assays, mass spectrometry, and PLK1 inhibitor experiments.

claim: Exogenously expressing S224E leads to colony formation defects.
source: As exogenously expressing S224E leads to colony formation defects and gene expression changes, our data hint at the importance of CTCF Ser224-P for proper cell function.
evidence: The claim is supported by colony size measurements.

claim: Exogenously expressing S224E leads to gene expression changes.
source: As exogenously expressing S224E leads to colony formation defects and gene expression changes, our data hint at the importance of CTCF Ser224-P for proper cell function.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Ser224 does not directly affect CTCF binding to DNA.
source: First, Ser224 does not directly affect CTCF binding to DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSA data showing that S224A and S224E mutants bind DNA similarly to wild-type CTCF.

claim: CTCF Ser224-P occupies a subset of all CTCF sites genome wide.
source: However, while CTCF Ser224-P occupies a subset of all CTCF sites genome wide, how this PTM is limited to a fraction of sites on the chromatids and pericentric satellites is still unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing fewer CTCF Ser224-P peaks than CTCF peaks.

claim: Overexpression of S224E does not lead to changes in TAD structure.
source: Second, while overexpression of a S224E leads to colony formation defects, we did not observe any changes in a TAD's structure, suggesting that CTCF Ser224-P may not impact the architectural role of CTCF, at least around the gene-rich Mecp2 TAD.
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C2 data showing similar TAD scores with or without S224E overexpression.

claim: Cell cycle progression of cells overexpressing the phospho-mimic S224E is not obviously affected.
source: Third, cell cycle progression and ploidy of cells overexpressing the phospho-mimic were not obviously affected.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle profile data.

claim: Ploidy of cells overexpressing the phospho-mimic S224E is not obviously affected.
source: Third, cell cycle progression and ploidy of cells overexpressing the phospho-mimic were not obviously affected.
evidence: The claim is supported by karyotyping data.

claim: Regulation of CTCF Ser224-P is needed to prevent dysregulation of hundreds of genes.
source: We conclude that regulation of CTCF Ser224-P is needed to prevent dysregulation of hundreds of genes, directly or indirectly through mechanisms that likely do not involve CTCF interphase binding, architectural function, cell cycle progression or ploidy.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed gene expression changes and the lack of effects on other cellular processes.

claim: CTCF interacts with cohesins.
source: For example, CTCF interacts with cohesins and the latter remain at the centromere to facilitate cohesion during metaphase (Rubio et al., 2008; Xiao et al., 2011; Stedman et al., 2008; Morales and Losada, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rubio et al., 2008; Xiao et al., 2011; Stedman et al., 2008; Morales and Losada, 2018.
